One of the greatest games of it's era.

If you're like me, a 90s baby, this game came out right at the peak of gaming.

This game was revolutionary. It came at the height of the war in the Middle East. It didn't matter if your parents were R or D. If they watched CNN or FOX. As a kid the war over there was in your face 24-7. On tv, at school, everywhere there was commentary on what was going on.

So, as a kid, to be able to have a game "put you in" the middle of a modern war was TOP TIER. The campaign was, and is, so good to play. The story is just so phenomenal. It made you feel like you were apart of a bigger national conflict.

The multiplayer was amazing too. It felt like every match you were apart of the "bigger conflict" in the background of the campaign. It also was revolutionary. Perks, killstreaks, game modes. It was all so new at the time. I had been playing online COD since COD 2. So the jump from those, to COD 4 was literally mind blowing. Activision at the time had struck gold.

If you weren't around during it's release, you won't understand how this game changed "the game". It wasn't afraid to push boundaries. It wasn't afraid to try something new. 

So, I got this on Steam to take a trip back down memory lane. The original MW trilogy is like an old friend. It never gets old.

The hackers got bored and went on to greener pastures.
All that is left is us game boomers.
Everyone is nice, everyone is just having fun. recommend you revisit for good wholesome fun and nostalgia.

I'm 42 and I'm playing the game for the first time. I wasn't expecting how good it is. I dare to say this is the best of the Modern Warfare series.

Singleplayer

Objectively:
The singleplayer can take between 5-10 hours to beat and runs without any issues on a modern PC. I managed to finish the entire campaign without a single crash, which is honestly impressive. The graphics have also aged very well, as they are stylized just enough to look realistic without constantly reminding you that this is an old game.

Subjectively:
The original Modern Warfare trilogy is one of my favorite franchises in all of gaming and thus the CoD4 campaign is a very nostalgic piece of art for me. The story is interesting and action-packed, yet the pacing is done so well that it managed to maintain my immersion for the entirety of the campaign. That being said (and having played the previous CoD games), I am well aware that CoD4 did not innovate on the shooter genre in terms of gameplay and storytelling, but in my humble opinion - it perfected it.

Multiplayer

Objectively:
Surprisingly active at the time of writing this review. Upon entering any server for the first time a mod will be installed (cod4x) which at the moment patches the game to version 20.1/20.5 and unlocks an abundance of new servers running on those patches. All game modes still have active servers with TDM and HC TDM being always active.

Subjectively:
CoD4 is among my favorite fps when it comes to multiplayer. I think it has some of the most diverse and memorable maps of the franchise, featuring both close-quarters and long-range sections on most of them, which makes all weapon types viable on the appropriate maps/sections. Most of the guns are usable and balanced, but in their own unique ways. For example take the AK-47, M16A4, M4 Carbine, and the G36C. These are popular and viable assault rifles that function very differently, yet can all yield the same results with the appropriate attachments and playstyle. The same can be said about the other weapon types, although results will vary depending on the map/game mode.

Should you buy?

100% if it's on sale, 80% if not :D Would be 100% regardless of sales, but the game lacks any form of cloud saving, so backing up and saving your multiplayer and singleplayer progress (in case you want to come back to it later) will have to be done manually. Also let's not forget that the multiplayer activity is due to community efforts and not on part of Activision or Infinity Ward, therefore giving them 20 euro (price without sale at the moment) for a 2007 game (albeit a good one) seems a bit too much considering your other options for the same price.

Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare is the series at its Finest Hour.
Back in 2007, it was a big year for video games, on PC we got Orange Box, Crysis, Bioshock,etc, console players had Halo 3, AC and Mass Effect, even among those big titles, Call of Duty 4 stood out. Its predecessors, namely Call of Duty and CoD2, were already highly successful, but CoD4 was simply beyond most gamers' expectation. I still remember playing this on my roommate's PC and got totally blown away by the "One shot, one kill" mission.

Singleplayer Story: 9/10
The story is straight forward, it is not a role-playing game where you made choices, or a Hollywood movie with lots of twists, you simply move with your squad, and shoot bad guys. However, the developer still manages to put the action pieces together with a nice story, it is not perfect, but can still give you the good old "Saving Private Ryan" feeling (like it was in MOHAA). In comparsion, MW2's story tries to give you "WOW" moments, like a Michael Bay movie with lots of cool actions, but fails to deliver the glorious feel.

Presentation: 9.5/10
The presentation is top notch in 2007, some moments are still amazing to this day, like the mission "All Ghillied Up" is an instant classic, where you crawled through emeny fields in a ghillied suit, with heavy tanks and patrols moving by, it is one of the most thrilling experiences in FPS history. The graphics are surely out-dated, but they aged elegantly. The gun models, animations and battlefield atomsphere are impeccable even in today's standards, which create great immersion. The pacing of shooting scene/intermission is perfect. There are also lots of explosions, but none feels out of place. 

Music: 9/10
The in-game music composed by Harry Gregson-Williams suits the pace and atomsphere perfectly, whether it is the middle-eastern showdown, or the desolate pripyat city, or the ICBM lauch field, the music always bring the scene to life. It may not surpass the later MW2's music by Hans Zimmer Team, but still excellent game soundtrack.

Multiplayer: 9.5/10
The MP mechanics was a revolution back in 2007, very fun and addictive even to this day. Most MP maps (aside from a few tiny maps) are well crafted to hold as much as 40-50 players, while still very fun to play with low player counts(8-16), also keep in mind that In later CoD (MW2 above) the player count is capped at 18, which, in my opinion, completely lost the epic battlefield feeling. This game also came before the crappy IWNet ever existed thus supports dedicated server, you can easily find a populated server with playable ping, without the worries about host-migration or host abuse, etc.
The weapons are balanced and diversified, not only feel great but actually have recoil(unlike those "laser guns" in later CoDs). The good old 3-5-7 killstreaks are simple and effective, as well as satisfying, you won't get ridiculous powerful killstreak (like nuke or AC-130 in later CoDs) but the result is still very rewarding.

End of the line
Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare is the prime CoD experience on PC. With so many blockbuster shooters flooding the market today, you may want to pay this old game a revisit, and see what we gamers have missed all those past years.

Edit: My steam profile suggests less than 1 hour CoD4 gameplay, which is not true. My in-game stats shows I played online for more than 500 hrs, coupled with another 300-400 hrs spent playing on mods, my total play time is nearly 1000 hrs. The reason is that I used Steam key on a retail copy to avoid Steam overlay/Punkbuster incompabilites. If you don't mind losing steam overlay, I suggest you do the same, the online gameplay will be much smoother.

I just want to confirm this for people wondering if this game is still alive. It totally is! Even after a decade, there are a TONNE of servers active with many players still playing on them. You dont need to download any mods or patches to make it work, nor do you need to even touch punkbuster. Not every single server will work because some require maps/files you may not have, but upon failing to connect, they usually give you a link to the site you can get them from. As for vanilla maps / gamemodes, this totally works!! No CD key bullshit, just select a server and connect! Leveling up your rank also functions just fine. In a single 30min TDM i ranked up a couple times so im not entirely sure if it was always that fast or if the server had boosted rates but it hardly matters as your rank is linked to a file on your PC. If you so choose, you can download a MP profile that has everything unlocked, or just enjoy ranking normally. 

If you know how, you can also port forward and host a live or dedicated server for you and friends right from the game's multiplayer menu. You can even make it public (show up on server browser) for others to join.

As for the single player aspect. It's one of the best of the series (story and gameplay wise). I've played Counterstrike for multiple years and often refused to get sunked into a CoD game despite trying many of them due to their weak 'feel good' style of gameplay katered towards a smaller skill gap however CoD4 has been the only exception for me, putting hundreds of hours on Xbox 360 souly for this game many years back. I've run through the story at least 5 times and enjoyed it every time since. It's dramatic, slightly cheesy at times but overall told very well and have solid characters you surely will get attached to. The system req's are quite low as well so nearly any PC from 06 with a 128mb GPU and Pentium 4 will be able to run this game at a solid 60. 

I'd strongly reccomend this game considering the community is still very much active. Even when the master server goes down, many 3rd party websites offer lists of live IP's you can directly connect to without the use of the server browser. $10 is totally worth it, I couldn't be happier.

[b]RCE (Remote Code Execution exploits) exist for this software[/b]. Activision does not care and has no reason to care. The modifications at hand are at best, a last resort, unfortunately the fate of old FPS games. Best to serve a dedicated server with your own "wild west" justice these days.

[h1]Explanations - Long Read Ahead![/h1]
Basically this link explains the RCE from a trusted source: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2018-20817

Basically data overflows create an opening for malicious actors to sneak code if you enter a lobby (custom, unprotected host migrations) that manipulates server downloads (packets) to execute malicious code executables/scripts. 

As much as I loved playing it at one point, look for anti-RCE patches on PCGAMINGWIKI. If a game doesn't have an ANTI-RCE patch, I do not recommend playing it until someone programs and releases one.

[WINDOWS 10-11]
It is critical that you patch Modern Warfare before playing online. Configuring your antivirus to protect your resident memory ("Isolation Protection") and other exploits should be enabled per profile for Modern Warfare.exe. Firewall rules should be correctly set such as not port forwarding and inbound connections set to block (and do not use public, use private connection). This will give a "just-in-case" protection.

If you do enter a lobby unprotected, you have a moderate to high chance of having your system become compromised. [b]Many videos show the RCE in effect on Youtube. From setting global speeds, aimbotting, significant manipulation of game mechanics to flat out crashing the game and slowhacking to full-on infecting peoples systems with malware [trojans/worms/viruses].[/b]

Black-hat hackers (hackers who purposely, maliciously access secure systems with intent to steal information and/or destroy data) can remotely access your system with TrustedInstaller privileges (access and change ANYTHING) which includes putting worms, trojans, keyloggers, malware and PUPs (Potentially Unwanted Programs like spyware/adware) - this can [b]open your system to essentially any form of attack! So backup as well![/b]

This means you could lose your data (such as stuff you create/stream or record/save games), bank details can be siphoned from your keypresses which could result in a loss of financial integrity/lost accounts, your computer could be used as a botnet (to infect other systems which could add to the problem at hand) and worse of all, if especially egregious cases, can actually ruin your system physically with low-level [b]ransomware[/b] which can [b]affect your bootloader(s)[/b], rendering the system completely inoperative.

[h1]Single Player Campaigns are OKAY to play unless Co-Op[/h1]

As long as you aren't connected to the internet via Peer to Peer (should have an offline mode or simply disable your ethernet and wifi adapter to be safe, you cannot be hacked if they cannot get an open physical port and/or wifi hotspot and thus your IP Addresses) you can play single-player campaigns with no fears.

Games with always online DRM may pose a risk but generally, the hackers would need to hack the master servers to gain access. If there has been a leak, backup sync files (use PCGAMINGWIKI to find directories or the save files location) and make haste in changing passwords immediately - use confusing combinations and write them down!

Even then, as long as you aren't joining insecure servers, keep in mind that co-op uses online peer-to-peer for host migration which could pose a risk so COD campaign co-op and COD:WAW:Zombies may still pose a penetration risk.

Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare set a new benchmark for first-person shooters when it launched, redefining the genre with its modern military setting and intense pacing. The game departed from its World War II roots to present a fast-paced, high-stakes narrative grounded in contemporary conflict. With its expertly designed missions and cinematic presentation, it quickly established itself as a standout title in the series. The sense of urgency and realism it offers remains impactful even years after its release.
The story follows a gripping narrative centered around global terrorism and military intervention, featuring perspectives from multiple characters across various factions. This approach offers a layered and immersive storytelling experience, moving players through war-torn environments and covert operations. Memorable missions such as “All Ghillied Up” showcase not only technical ingenuity but also emotional depth. The narrative structure successfully keeps players engaged through its tense pacing and dramatic twists.
Gameplay in Modern Warfare is tight, responsive, and highly refined, delivering a balance between cinematic spectacle and strategic combat. The combination of on-rails sequences, tactical objectives, and large-scale battles ensures a dynamic experience. Multiplayer mode became a defining element, introducing the now-iconic progression system with perks, killstreaks, and customizable loadouts. Its addictiveness and replayability set a new standard for competitive online shooters.
Visually, the game was a technical marvel for its time, utilizing realistic lighting, detailed character models, and immersive environments. The attention to visual fidelity helped ground the experience in a believable modern warfare setting. Effects such as smoke, fire, and debris added intensity to every combat encounter. The art direction and animations contributed to a polished and authentic look that supported the game’s tone.
Overall, Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare delivers an exceptional blend of storytelling, gameplay, and visual execution. Its influence on the FPS genre is undeniable, thanks to its innovative design choices and gripping presentation. From its emotionally charged narrative to its groundbreaking multiplayer mechanics, it stands as a milestone in gaming history. This title remains a prime example of how to elevate a franchise while pushing industry standards.
Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare gets an 8/10.

Please do not treat that abomination as a replacement for CoD4, or let it represent anything CoD4 is in any way.  MWR only shows how far this series has fallen.  It's recommended to just pick this game up instead, under any circumstances.

That out of the way, CoD4 runs well enough.  The game runs almost without a hitch, with expectedly excellent framerates (no fps cap), it's well-optimized, and it still looks good enough while doing so.  The sounds are all excellent, from the sporadic music to the sound effects that help understand everything going on in battle.  I can't remember the last crash I had with this game, and that includes running this on both Windows 7 and 10.  One will hardly run into issues when playing.  And if you're like me, you'll be playing a lot -- especially its multiplayer.

Joe Maddon, manager of the Chicago Cubs, routinely tells baseball players to, "Do simple better."  This is what CoD4's multiplayer does best when compared to later releases.  This game doesn't have as many weapons or killstreaks as later CoDs, it may not have modern graphics or fancy gun skins, nor does it have the ranking system and prestige system of other CoDs.  However, unlike later games in the series, CoD4 does all the basics very well.  The game works as it should, without much game-engine lag.  Connections actually work, because online matches are supported by servers that also actually work.  To add to that, a nice touch is that the DLC maps for this game come with CoD4 on Steam, so the playerbase is never fragmented.  Frag x3 and maybe Martyrdom aside, no perks or guns are overbearingly overpowered in this game.  This includes the killstreaks, which is a simple 3-5-7 setup.  This game just WORKS, and it's still so much fun.

However, in 2018, people may have some issues trying to find an experience that works for them.  A downside to this game is the extreme unreliability of the in-game server browser, which confuses many.  Personally, I avoid that altogether and instead use a third-party website like Gametracker to find actual, legitimate servers that run this game.  From there, I nab the IP address of the server desired and punch it in the console command to connect.  This is much more reliable, and I hope this helps a lot of people.  Third-party, player-owned dedicated servers are still far better for immediately dealing with cheaters anyways, instead of how Activision and the various CoD devs handle cheating today (just look at CoD WW2, what a joke).  And while not all game modes are supported 10 years later after its launch, there's plenty of servers still standing that give good enough competition.  There are many more players that still play CoD4 than MWR today, as well.  In essence, learn the /connect console command, and anyone can get a good game in still.

I've been playing CoD4's multiplayer for over 10 years, but I never touched its single-player campaign until last week.  And while the multiplayer is still the main draw of this game, the campaign is quite fun here.  The story is tense, the levels put you in many types of situations, the difficulty is well-balanced, and there are plenty of collectibles to find for completionists looking for replay value.  There were only a couple moments that I could see be difficult on Veteran difficulty, but nothing terribly impossible to overcome.  Overall, the story is a good diversion for a lazy afternoon.  As someone who perfers MP over SP by a long shot, I had a lot of fun with it.

Over two years ago, I got sick and tired of newer CoDs constantly dropping the ball over making a legitimately fun and functional game.  That's why I picked CoD4 up on PC, and I've been having fun with this game ever since.  As long as people keep playing this classic, I'll still be having fun with Call of Duty.  I can still recommend this game, and it's still my favorite Call of Duty game in the series.

Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare is arguably where the series turned from a good game into a great game, and became the behemoth franchise it is today. At one time, beginning around the release of this title, the hype around the series and the games really was justified: it is easy to forget that COD4 was competing against massive releases such as Halo 3 and came out on top (yes, it was sold on more platforms but still).

It is worth it just for the single player alone. With no real connection to previous titles (beyond the name Price), the campaign follows a similar split between playing as either a British or American soldier, but set in the modern day (or at least modern at time of release - 2011). There were aspects of the game which were entirely new at the time, especially the grenade physics and bullet penetration: cover was no longer secure, you cannot sit behind a cardboard box and expect to be safe. While seemingly insignificant, this was a major change and step forward for realism. The campaign also includes some of the most memorable levels in any game, such as All Ghillied Up, or the scene immediately following the rescue of the Black Hawk pilot (not something someone will ever forget playing for the first time).

Where the game truly shone however was multiplayer: it was a game changer for the series. Not only were classes, levelling, attachments and perks added in, as well as the persistent bullet penetration and grenade physics from the campaign, but it also included some of the greatest maps ever made. Many are deserving of their status: Crossfire, Vacant, District, Backlot, Strike and of course the daddy of them all - Crash. This may be the only Call of Duty game I have played where there does not seem to be a truly terrible, avoid at all costs map (even if not all of them are quite so great). The game also went viral (before viral was a thing) with the release of Promod: essentially a competitively focused mod for the game with the aim of making it as balanced and fair as possible (limited weapons/perks and maps). If you wish to get into the game today and start playing, this is the way to go. Promod can be found on their Github page at [url]https://github.com/promod/promod4[/url] - there are still active servers. Thankfully, a lot of the annoying stuff such as martyrdom and last stand are taken out, making it an altogether more "pure" experience.

Call of Duty 4 is perhaps the most influential game in the already-influential FPS series, and not without reason. It propelled the series to new heights, generating a wave of sequels that would eventually enshrine it as the repetitive, generic, overrated military shooter franchise that soured some on the entire genre. In its day, CoD4 was none of those things, and it still holds up as one of the best Modern Warfare games ever made. This is mainly because of its stellar singleplayer that blends the quotidian feel of earlier [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/trar/recommended/2630/]WWII CoD games[/url] with an action movie sensibility that wasn't overdone supersoldier crap like its sequels.


By the time of those later Modern Warfare games, the campaigns had come to be regarded as perfunctory training courses for the multiplayer. This attitude had spread to other games trying to ride CoD's coattails, most prominently the Battlefield series, which in the early 2010s went from games with great singleplayer that complimented the multiplayer (Bad Company 2) to games with awful singleplayer (Battlefield 3). I don't blindly hate multiplayer or anything, but as a lover of good singleplayer campaigns, this was a trend that had concerned me greatly. I'm very glad to say that CoD4's campaign is pretty much as good as they said it was.

I'll briefly address the core gameplay. The feel of the guns is just great and the whole game is smooth, which it must be admitted is something Call of Duty has mastered, no matter what one has to say about it. It's the superb gunplay that underpins the whole experience and contributes to making it such a great shooter.

From start to finish, the whole campaign is a slick ride. While it's a bit shorter than the WWII games that preceded it, it's even more cinematic than they ever were, and manages to place you in a number of unique and memorable gameplay situations that keep things interesting. I would have liked a little bit more context regarding what kind of country the Middle Eastern sections of the game take place in beyond "there was a revolution" - the intro car ride seems to imply it was against the Saudi monarchy, which was then itself deposed by one of the game's antagonists. Some more context from the sociopolitical landscape would have been nice if only to establish a sense of place in the game's world, but the story still ultimately works.

More importantly, the story as a whole isn't a bunch of technothriller nonsense. ([i]That[/i] would start to creep in with Modern Warfare 2.) The antagonists have believable motives for the heinous acts they commit, acts that are themselves more believable than the plotting of villains later in the series, and the geopolitical situation that IS depicted isn't completely idiotic. As an aside, it takes place far enough in the past from now that I consider it something of an alternate history.

The campaign's depiction of modern warfare also allows it to depict the vulnerability of individual soldiers, especially at the end of Act 1. One of the POV characters is a special forces soldier and consequently more immune to this, but not completely immune, and it's ultimately necessary to keep the story moving along, so I can live with that.

All this, [i]in addition[/i] to fun multiplayer, is why I consider CoD4 one of the best games in the series that takes place after 1945.

Of course, nothing's perfect. The main problem is that endlessly spawning enemies make some sections more of a challenge than they should be. They were definitely more noticeable than in CoD2, at least. While I guess it encourages more aggressive play as in CoD2, it didn't exactly do me any favors given my more tactical playstyle. For all the sins later games committed, the series thankfully stopped doing the endless enemy thing after Black Ops 1.


Multiplayer is still somewhat active, and introduces most of the things CoD multiplayer is famous for, such as XP, killstreaks, and perks. Sprinting arrives in its most recognizable form, whereas CoD 2 didn't have it at all. It even had weapon skins and customizable loadsouts before Team Fortress 2 ever did.

It's arcadey, chaotic and just plain fun. Don't expect Rainbow Six Siege or Insurgency - it's pretty brainless, and I can definitely see how the seeds of CoD MP's downfall into ADHD killstreak spam for elementary schoolers were sown with this game. Overall, it's a nice addition for those who enjoyed the singleplayer, and unlike later CoD tiles it's not the only good thing about the game.

Despite the speedy nature of combat, there are still lean buttons, and they're surprisingly not entirely useless from a tactical standpoint. Weirdly, there is no Steam cloud storage for player profiles, meaning if you start playing on one computer and then install the game on another, you'll have to manually port your profile data or start from the bottom.

Given that most players are already at max rank (the game is more than a decade old after all), and that a number of guns/perks/attachments require certain levels to be achieved, I'd say finding a way to boost it if you want is fair. However, you lose the experience of progressing through the ranks normally by doing so - I was annoyed to find the very first server I joined was a "high XP" server that essentially gave me a bunch of stuff for minimal effort.


Would I recommend Call of Duty 4? If you like FPS games in any capacity, [b]yes[/b]. Play it for the campaign, at the absolute least. You won't regret it. I wouldn't recommend the remastered version over this one, not right now at least. Not only is it more expensive, and not only is the multiplayer dead and filled with lootboxes, it's also much more taxing on computers, which may be a concern if your machine is on the modest side.

I have also put a decent amount of time into it's PC version so I feel very confident in my earlier statement regarding this particular game. I also have found that despite what followed after this title's release, it is still the best game in the entire franchise. The story is absolutely iconic. It's mission structure and sequencing are perfect. It's visuals have a slight cartoonish yet gritty 2000's edge that emanates pure artistic sauce. It's characters and dialogue birthed the most critically acclaimed sub franchise of a video game series that I can think of in recent times. It's weapon sandbox was absolutely stellar introducing what would become fan favorites such as the AK47, MP5 and M16 to the franchise and delivering a fleshed out arsenal of modern day weapons alongside the earlier mentioned givens to really drive player choice with the pacing of the game's combat. And it's combat? It's moment to moment gameplay? Absolutely revolutionized first person shooters as we know it, and ushered in the now depressing age of modern gaming. And it could be played online. And it was peak. I could go on about the legendary map design or the revolutionary create a class system with the personal XP progression system and prestige and the camos and the perks and the game modes but since it is all still currently online on PC via a super duper easy client patch you should just see for yourself. Despite what anti consumer business practices this franchise's overwhelming success would eventually allow into this industry through greed and assembly line bare minimum effort yearly released "premium" titles, Call of Duty 4 Modern Warfare was and still is peak, and if you have not played it you need to correct that.

[b]PROS:[/b]
+ cool epic campaign
+ fun gameplay
+ no cut-out DLC
+ no microtransactions
+ mod support

[b]CONS:[/b]
- aged graphics (compared to the remastered version)

- cheaters in multiplayer

[b]Comment:[/b]
Remembering the old days of playing this game got me to re-buy it again, just to have it and to see if it would work on my PC. A comparison with the remastered version cannot be avoided. While the remaster looks a LOT better it is tainted with greedy Activision decisions. Like selling a map pack for more than it cost originally (and this map pack is free with the classic PC version now) or adding microtransactions. The campaign is pretty much legendary at this point. Who could forget levels like the nuke mission or being a sniper in Ukraine! Yes, it is over-the-top a lot of the times but that what made it fun back then. This game spawned a generation of modern shooters (including it's own sequels) that tried to grab the charm of this game. Some were better, a lot of them worse, but this was the first one and so it became a classic. Still plenty of people playing multiplayer for such an old game. Choice of servers is between PunkBuster on or off (don't forget to refresh). Without it you have less of a hassle (no need to go find PB configs) but also can expect cheaters more often. There is a system of ranks and challenges present which can occupy you in multiplayer a bit longer. There are also mods so check some of them out if you want. Overall this is a cool game that aged in graphics but certainly not in how much fun it is. Worth a try for the campaign and if you have the patience/friends also for the multiplayer.

Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare is the first game of the series to break away from the tried and true World War 2 setting and into the new era of war, involving constant risks of nuclear annihilation and smaller scale, urban combat. Russia has fallen into civil war as Ultra-nationalists attempt to resurrect the Soviet Union, meanwhile an unnamed Middle Eastern country has been overthrown by a warlord with ties to said Ultra-Nationalists. We play as two main characters, one a US Marine called Paul Jackson and a British SAS Sergeant named John “Soap” MacTavish. Starting off we play as Soap who has just been accepted into a SAS squad led by series’ famous and mustached hero, John Price.

You are tasked with completing some quick practice training before being briefed on your mission to familiarize you with the game. If you have played any Call of Duty game or any FPS in general over the past decade you will have no issues getting the hang of it. Introduced in this tutorial is the new feature of flash grenades designed to disorient enemies caught in its blast. Mastering these will greatly improve your chances of survival since you will now be fighting in small areas instead of the vast battlefields of WW2 and a well-placed throw can decide the outcome. By far my favorite edition is that bullets can now pass through thin objects which makes it a ton of fun as bullets penetrate all your surroundings, causing you to desperately seek cover behind something sensible.

It works the other way around as well so no longer will enemies by able to use a tiny fence as indestructible cover. With that new found knowledge found in your training you are then briefed on your mission to retrieve an object from a well-guarded enemy cargo ship. It is here that you realize that the CoD series has taken a new feel to it. While previous games were more down to earth and grim with the sight of allies being killed being common place, Modern Warfare goes the Michael Bay route with tons of explosions, escaping a flooding cargo ship and jumping into the helicopter at the very last second. It's not a criticism nor a necessarily bad thing but it's a change of tone I felt was worth mentioning.

The journey of playing both US and British forces take you all over Russia and the Middle East, both stories are interconnected and give you a greater view of the story instead of being there for convenient teleportation to another cool location. You play as a few other unnamed soldiers, pilots and even John Price for a bit though those are over very quickly and are just keep the game from getting stale by changing up the gameplay such as you having to provided air support and carefully shooting your missiles. Most of these extra characters feel gimmicky and are not really all that fun except for when you play as Price in Chernobyl, on an important stealth mission. That was easily the high point of the game and a moment I will remember long after I stop playing. And that is saying something as there are many high points when playing as the main protagonists.

Aside from bullet penetration, the gameplay is the same as previous entries only now you have newer weaponry, gadgets and gun attachments such as a grenade launcher added under your assault rifle. Smoke grenades are back and as useful as ever to pass through heavy fire or be concealed from tanks and such. Another new addition that is extremely gimmicky and neigh on useless are the night vision goggles. You could see just fine without them and don't really serve any purpose other than a bullet point on the new features list. You're never in a position where you have to scavenge for items or ammo, they are refilled after every mission or taken away, you will always have what you need which makes sense considering these elite soldiers won't go in unprepared but feels too “hand holdy” gameplay wise.

Especially when it comes to ammo. You are given an obscene amount and I have never once had to switch weapons or take an enemies weapon. That was one change to the series I did not like as you will not use any of the other weapons in the game unless you go out of your way to do so while playing through the campaign. Melee combat has been changed a bit as well, while the previous games had you use your weapons to smack an enemy, Modern Warfare has you automatically pull out a knife and lunge at him which I personally find much more satisfying. The smaller environments both harm and help Modern Warfare, on one hand it is far more obvious how linear the game is but on the other it makes it more in your face and fast paced than ever before.

The campaign is short but sweet, it took me about 5 hours to fully complete though it went at break neck speedy action every step of the way and had a shockingly decent story. There is not much motivation to replay it though. 30 enemy laptops are scattered throughout the campaign and unlock cheat codes after finding enough of them yet the cheat codes are usually very underwhelming such as making your screen black and white or other pointless screen effects. The only cheat code that I've unlocked that was decent was the “Cluster grenade” which causes huge explosions once your grenades detonates. To try to motivate you to reply they also added an Arcade Mode once you finish the game that lets you replay any mission and earn points for everything you do. It offers nothing but racking up high scores and is nowhere near enough to get me to replay the campaign after just having finished it.

Where the game really shined back in the day was in its multiplayer. It's RPG like progression system to unlock titles, weapons and perks was revolutionary and changed the FPS genre as a whole. For better or for worse is in the eye of the beholder. It introduced the problem that those who played longer have a significant advantage over newer players but on the other hand it is satisfying to be constantly rewarded with stuff for playing and helped differentiate each player. One may have a perk that allows them to run further without stopping, another may simply have more health and yet another player may be able to hip fire far more accurately and surprise you. It makes every firefight interesting since you never know just what tricks your foe has up his/her sleeve. Once you hit level 5 you can build up to five custom classes that will be useful for different situations and tons of fun to experiment with.

Be warned though, the multiplayer will crash on start unless right click on your sound icon, go into your recording tab and then enable “Stereo Mix”. No clue as to why but that fixes the issue. Another issue is that if you are playing via Steam make sure to unbind the in-game screenshot key that defaults to F12 as that will also cause your game to crash if you take a screen-shot. Weird steps to make the multiplayer work but it is definitely still worth playing even after all these years and still has a decently sized community so finding a game won't be a problem (as of this review). In a rather cool move by Activision the 1 DLC pack released for Modern Warfare is already included. All in all, Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare was a breath of fresh air and finally broke the series free from it's done to death WW2 roots.
